craft_claim: Compassion is action-oriented and assumes shared vulnerability, whereas pity is hierarchical and distancing and can serve the observer's sentiment, so the compassionate voice must not place the sufferer beneath the speaker.

supporting_evidence.location: Upheavals of Thought, ch. 6, compassion as a cognitive/eudaimonistic judgement
supporting_evidence.note: Nussbaum analyzes compassion as a judgement that another's suffering is serious, undeserved, and relevant to one's own flourishing, with an assumption of similar possibilities; this distinguishes it from pity's condescension.

supporting_evidence.location: On Revolution, chapter on the social question (compassion vs pity)
supporting_evidence.note: Arendt distinguishes compassion, which is directed at a particular sufferer, from pity, which can be generalized and enjoyed as an emotion of the observer.

counterevidence.note: The compassion/pity distinction is interpretive and contested across the philosophical literature; there is no single canonical empirical test, so confidence is moderate.

scope: Narrator stance toward a sufferer in essay, reportage, and narrative.
exceptions: Ironic or satirical uses that deliberately stage pity in order to critique it.
